scenes.narration: Eleven point eight cents. Out of every dollar Americans spend on food, that is all that ends up with the farm that grew it.

scenes.narration: And the supermarket? One of America's biggest grocers kept less than two cents of profit on every dollar of sales. So if the farmer gets a dime, and the store gets a couple of pennies, where does the rest of your money go?
And why did the bill at the checkout jump so much in just a few years?
By the end of this video, you will know who takes each slice of your food dollar, why prices spiked, and why regulators and grocers still argue about who profited.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Every year, the Department of Agriculture takes one dollar of American food spending and splits it into pieces. It counts both groceries and restaurant meals. And it asks a simple question. Who earned each cent along the way?

The farm comes first, but its share is surprisingly small. In twenty twenty-four, the farm share was eleven point eight cents. The other eighty-eight point two cents paid for everything that happens after the farm gate.

Food processing, turning wheat into bread and cattle into steaks, took sixteen point one cents. Wholesalers, the middlemen who move food to stores, took six point three cents. Transportation and storage, four point one cents. Energy, three point one cents. Advertising, two point two cents.

Grocery stores and other food retailers took thirteen point eight cents. And the biggest slice of all went to food services, restaurants and cafeterias, with thirty-eight point six cents. Much of what we pay for food is not the food. It is the cooking, the serving, the shelves and the trucks.

Let me draw your food dollar. Here is one dollar. The farm gets a thin slice on the left, about twelve cents. Then processing. Then wholesale and trucks. Then the grocery store. And the biggest piece, restaurants. Most of the dollar is spent after the food leaves the farm.

keyframes.cue: The farm gets a thin slice

scenes.narration: Those slices are fairly stable from year to year. The price of the whole dollar is not. And a few years ago, it started climbing fast.

scenes.narration: By our calculation from Labor Department data, grocery prices are up about thirty-two percent since January twenty twenty. The Department of Agriculture says twenty twenty-two was the worst year, when food prices overall rose nine point nine percent, the biggest yearly jump in its chart of food prices.

Eggs became the symbol. A dozen large eggs cost about a dollar forty-six in January twenty twenty. In March twenty twenty-five, the average price hit six dollars and twenty-three cents. The main reason, according to the Department of Agriculture, was an outbreak of bird flu that began in twenty twenty-two and hit egg farms again and again.

Then supply came back. By September twenty twenty-six, the same dozen cost about two dollars and twenty-seven cents. The Department of Agriculture expects egg prices to fall by almost thirty percent this year.

Beef went the other way, and it kept going. A pound of ground beef cost three dollars and eighty-nine cents in January twenty twenty. In August twenty twenty-six, it cost six dollars and ninety-two cents. And beef prices are forecast to rise another eight point seven percent this year.

Overall, the surge has slowed. In the twelve months to September twenty twenty-six, grocery prices rose one point eight percent. The forecast for this year is two point three percent, below the long-run average of two point six percent a year. But slower growth is not the same as lower prices. The higher level stays.

Let me draw the two kinds of price rises. Eggs went up like a rocket, and came back down when the supply returned. Beef climbed like a staircase, step after step. And the whole grocery bill moved like a ramp. It flattened out, but it never went back down.

scenes.narration: So when prices jumped, many shoppers blamed the stores. But to judge that, you need to know how a supermarket actually makes money.

keyframes.label: …so how does a supermarket make money?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Take Kroger, one of the largest supermarket chains in America. In its twenty twenty-four fiscal year, it sold about one hundred and forty-seven billion dollars of goods, and kept about two point seven billion as profit. By our calculation, that is about one point eight cents on every dollar. The next year, a big write-down pushed it below one cent.

Albertsons, its rival, reported a net margin of one point two percent in fiscal twenty twenty-four. The industry's trade group, FMI, puts the average net profit for food retailers in twenty twenty-five at two point one percent. Those are thin numbers, even by the standards of retail.

So how do grocers survive? Volume and speed. A store makes a tiny amount on each sale, but it sells enormous amounts, and it sells the same products again every week. Walmart's American stores sold about two hundred and eighty-five billion dollars of groceries in its last fiscal year.

Let me draw a grocer's dollar. Most of it pays for the products on the shelf. Then wages, rent, electricity, trucks and card fees. What is left at the bottom, the profit, is a sliver. About two cents. Sell enough dollars, and two cents becomes billions.

scenes.narration: That is the industry's side of the story. But the government looked at the same years, and saw something different.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In twenty twenty-four, the Federal Trade Commission published a report on the grocery supply chain during the pandemic. It found that retailer revenues rose to more than six percent over their total costs in twenty twenty-one, higher than their last peak in twenty fifteen. And in the first part of twenty twenty-three, they reached seven percent.
But the FTC added an important caveat. It did not test whether specific companies raised their prices by more than their own costs went up.

The grocers' trade group tells it differently. It says food retailer profit margins fell from two point three percent in twenty twenty-two to one point six percent in twenty twenty-three, back to pre-pandemic levels. The two sides are using different measures, so both can be accurate at the same time. The argument is about what they mean.

There is also a price rise that does not look like one. When a package gets smaller but the price stays the same, the Labor Department counts the price per ounce. In its own example, a sixty-four ounce carton cut to sixty ounces at the same price counts as a six point seven percent price increase. Shrinkflation is in the numbers. It is just hidden on the label.

Let me draw the two measures. On the left, the FTC's view, revenue compared with all costs, across the whole industry. On the right, the grocers' view, net profit as a share of sales. Same years, different rulers. That is why the debate never ends.

scenes.narration: Margins are only half the question. The other half is how many companies are left to compete.

keyframes.label: Margins are only half the question…

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Look at beef. According to the Department of Agriculture, the four largest meatpackers handle eighty-five percent of all the cattle bought for beef, counted as steers and heifers. In nineteen eighty, the top four had thirty-six percent. A rancher selling cattle has only a handful of buyers to choose from.

Supermarkets tried to get bigger too. Kroger planned to buy its rival Albertsons for twenty-four point six billion dollars. The combined company would have had more than five thousand stores. The FTC sued to block it. In December twenty twenty-four, a federal court stopped the deal, and both companies walked away. Albertsons is now suing Kroger over the breakup.

Then there is the shelf itself. Stores often charge food makers for space, called slotting fees. In a study of a few product categories, the FTC found the average fee per item, for one retailer in one city, ranged from two thousand three hundred and thirteen dollars to twenty-one thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight dollars. That study is from two thousand three, but the practice is still around.

And the stores have a weapon of their own. Store brands. According to the private label industry's trade group, they made up twenty-one point three percent of grocery dollar sales in twenty twenty-five. When the store makes its own cereal, it competes with the brands on its own shelves.

Let me draw the funnel. At the top, many farms and ranches. In the middle, a few big processors. Then a few big grocery chains. At the bottom, millions of shoppers. The narrower the middle of the funnel, the more power sits there.

keyframes.cue: Then a few big grocery chains
keyframes.label: strokes[2].start.cue

scenes.narration: So what is the hidden business behind your grocery bill? It is not one villain. The farmer gets about twelve cents. The store keeps a couple of pennies. Most of your money pays for everything in between, the processing, the trucks, the shelves and the people. Some of the biggest jumps came when something in that long chain broke, like a flock of hens or a herd of cattle. The real question is how much power sits in the narrow parts of the chain.
